chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', from Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him) — he said:

I asked him, and I said: 'Has God delegated the matter to the servants?' He said: 'God is mightier than that.' I said: 'So did He compel them to commit disobediences?' He said: 'God is more just and wiser than that.'

He (the narrator) said, then he (the Imam) said: 'God said: O son of Adam! I have a closer claim to your good deeds than you, and you have a closer claim to your evil deeds than Me. You committed the disobediences through My strength which I placed in you.'

key_terms.أَمْرٌ بَيْنَ الْأَمْرَيْنِ: 'Amr bayn al-amrayn — the middle position between jabr and tafwid, the classical Shia doctrine on free will
key_terms.تَفْوِيض: Tafwid — divine delegation of all matters to human beings (rejected as implying limitation of God's power)
key_terms.جَبْر: Jabr — divine compulsion of human actions (rejected as contradicting God's justice)
key_terms.حَدِيثٌ قُدْسِيٌّ: Hadith Qudsi — a divine saying narrated by the Prophet or Imam in God's first person, distinct from Quranic text
key_terms.حَسَنَات: Hasanat — good deeds, acts of obedience
key_terms.سَيِّئَات: Sayyi'at — evil deeds, acts of disobedience

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia Islamic position on free will versus divine compulsion (jabr and tafwid)?
ai.summary: In this hadith, the narrator al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha' describes a conversation with Imam al-Ridha (AS) about the fundamental theological question of divine compulsion (jabr) versus divine delegation (tafwid). The Imam denies both extremes — God neither forces human beings into sin (which would contradict His justice) nor completely delegates affairs to them (which would imply limitation in His power). The Imam concludes with a divine saying (hadith qudsi) articulating the middle position: God has a greater claim to human good deeds, but humans bear the responsibility for their own sins, which they commit using the God-given capacity for action. This represents the classical Shia theological doctrine of 'amr bayn al-amrayn' (a matter between the two matters), rejecting both Mu'tazilite absolute free will and Ash'arite divine compulsion.

en.hubeali:
Al Husayn Bin Muhammad, from Moalla Bin Muhammad, from Al Hassan Bin Ali Al Washha, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Al-Hassan Al-Reza<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘

I asked him<sup>asws</sup>, so I said, ‘Does Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Delegate the matters to the servants?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is Mightier than that’. I said, ‘So does He<sup>azwj</sup> Compel them upon the disobedience?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is more Just and Wise than that’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘Then he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Said: “O son of Adam<sup>as</sup>! I<sup>azwj</sup> am closer with your good deeds than you are, and you are closer with your evil deeds than I<sup>azwj</sup> am. You are doing the disobediences by My<sup>azwj</sup> (Given) Strength which I<sup>azwj</sup> Made to be in you”’.
